newsitem.title: FRANCE: France and world mourn oceanographer Cousteau.
newsitem.headline: France and world mourn oceanographer Cousteau.

text.p: French oceanographer Jacques-Yves Cousteau, who revealed the mysteries of the seas in prize-winning films and fought for environmental causes around the world, died on Wednesday at the age of 87.
His widow Francine said he died of a heart attack at 2.30 a.m. (0030 GMT) at their Paris home while recovering from a respiratory ailment which had kept him in hospital for months.
She told a news conference he was conscious and lucid to his last day and had just completed a book to sum up his legacy.
Tributes poured in for the hawk-nosed, emaciated-looking man who was explorer, ecologist, teacher, film-maker and inventor wrapped together.

President Jacques Chirac mourned him as an "enchanter", saying he was probably the best known Frenchman worldwide for his pioneering films ranging from the Antarctic ice shelf to the blue lagoons of coral atolls.
U.S. Vice President Al Gore called him "a hero to men, women and children all over the world" and "a giant in every respect".
More tributes flowed at an Earth Summit at the United Nations, and from the environmental group Greenpeace.

"Captain Jacques-Yves Cousteau has gone to the Silent World this Wednesday, June 25, 1997," Cousteau's foundation said. A memorial service will be held in Paris' Notre-Dame cathedral on Monday but the foundation did not say where he would be buried.

"The Silent World" was the name of a documentary that won the top award at the Cannes film festival in 1956 and earned Cousteau world fame. The film was made with skin-diving gear co-invented by Cousteau in 1943, freeing divers from heavy helmets so they could float as if in space.

In his trademark sea-blue tunic and red beret, Cousteau became internationally famous through his books and films, particularly the U.S.-sponsored television series "The Undersea World of Jacques-Yves Cousteau," first broadcast in 1965.
Cousteau, who spoke English with a thick French accent, toured the world in the Calypso, a converted British minesweeper equipped with a marine laboratory.

The Calypso sank in Singapore last year, and Cousteau's 52-year-old widow vowed to pursue his efforts to build a Calypso II to be "the planet's look-out for the next 50 years". Plans are ready for the 61-metre (200 ft) ship, equipped with the 26-metre-tall (85 ft) metal "turbosails" he invented.

Her voice breaking, Francine read Cousteau's favourite verses, by French poet Paul Eluard: "To earth, to earth all that swims/To earth, to earth all that flies/I need the fish to carry my crown/I need the birds to speak to the crowd."

From the Antarctic -- huddled up watching penguins in a snowstorm -- to the Amazon or the depths of oceans surrounded by colourful fish, Cousteau won a worldwide reputation as a champion of the environment.
An ex-navy officer who won the Legion of Honour for spying on occupying Italian forces during World War Two, he was regularly voted France's most-loved public figure in polls.
Expressing "great sadness", Chirac said: "This former navy officer was in the tradition of the ocean explorers whose life seems so like a legend."
In one of his last campaigns, Cousteau joined international protests against Chirac's nuclear testing in the South Pacific in 1995.
Socialist French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin said: "The planet has lost one of its best known defenders."

The newspaper Le Monde hailed Cousteau as "Captain of the Oceans" and, drawing on Hemingway, entitled his career "The Old Man and the Sea". It quoted him as having said: "In life, there are two vital liquids -- water and money. You have to use both."

Cousteau, who acquired his first rudimentary movie camera at the age of nine, won a string of prizes for his films, including three Oscars and three awards at Cannes. Detractors called him a publicity-seeker with little scientific training.

He fell out with one of his sons, Jean-Michel, over alleged trademark infringements. Jean-Michel used the "Cousteau" name in a Fiji Islands resort. The case was settled last year under a deal in which "Jean-Michel" was added to the name.
The elder Cousteau's most recent invention was a wind-powered vessel with smokestack-like devices which suck in air currents and redirect them through vents and vanes to propel the craft forward.
Born on June 11, 1910, in the southwestern wine-growing region of Bordeaux, Cousteau spent his childhood in Paris and New York and studied at the naval academy in Brest, France.
